gloss: A river mouth the sea has walked up, so the water is salt a long way inland.
A dark mouth in the cliff foot that the tide fills twice a day and empties again.
A rib of rock the waves have holed clean through, still standing on two legs.
A pillar left offshore when the arch beside it fell; birds own the top of it.
A hole in the cliff top that spits spray and thunder whenever a big swell comes in.
A narrow slot cut back into the cliff along a weak seam, loud with water at the far end.
A flat shelf of scoured rock below the cliff, bare at low water and slick with weed.
An old shoreline stranded above the present one, level enough to build a road on.
A neck of sand and shingle joining an island to the shore; it drowns on the big tides.
A finger of shingle the drift keeps building out across open water, growing every year.
A bank of sand grown right across a bay mouth, shutting the water in behind it.
A low ridge of sand lying offshore, taking the weather so the mainland does not.
Shallow brackish water penned behind a bar, calm when the sea outside is not.
Where the river's water and the sea's argue twice a day over the same mudflats.
A blunt triangle of shingle thrown out from the coast where two drifts meet.
Shell sand blown inland and gone to grass; grazing on top of what was once a beach.
A band of rounded cobbles well above the waterline, from a sea that has since dropped.
Ground that is mud at low water and sea at high, with no clear edge between them.
A shoulder of cliff shoved out into the water; the coast road goes over it or not at all.
A stream that runs off the cliff lip and never reaches a beach, because there is none.
The river gives up and splits, laying its load down in a fan of shifting channels.
A wide bed of gravel bars where the river runs in a dozen shallow threads at once.
Flat ground ribbed with the ghosts of old bends the river has already abandoned.
A cut-off loop of river left standing on its own, going quietly green at the edges.
A spread of stone and grit laid out where a steep stream hits the flat and slows.
A low natural bank along the water, built from what the floods dropped first.
A dry step above the present river, cut when the water ran higher than it does now.
A deep scoured basin under a fall, cold and loud, with an undercut behind the water.
A steep-walled reach where the river is still cutting its way down through hard rock.
A long cut with the sky in a strip overhead and no way out for miles either side.
The dry tongue of ground between two rivers, just before they become one.
A wooded island the river has split around and not yet decided to take back.
A stream that runs into a hole in the ground and does not come out anywhere near.
A gravel shallow where the river spreads wide enough to walk, in the right season.
One unbroken backbone of rock; the only ways over it are the notches.
A peak with three clean faces meeting at a point, and nothing above it for a long way.
The low saddle between two summits: the crossing everyone uses, and everyone watches.
A shoulder running down off the main ridge, easy walking until it steepens.
A long hill with one gentle back and one abrupt face, like a wave about to break.
A sharp ridge of tilted strata standing at the same steep angle on both sides.
A table of ground standing above everything else, flat on top and cliffed all round.
The last stump of a table left standing after the rest of it wore away.
The cliffed edge where the high ground stops and the low country begins.
A cone of loose stone piled under a gully, sliding underfoot at every step.
A skirt of broken blocks below a cliff, from small chips to house-sized.
A stripe of scoured, treeless ground where the snow comes down every winter.
A shallow dip in a ridge line, the only place to cross without using hands.
The wooded rise between the plain and the real mountains, cut by short steep valleys.
A single great swell of rock with all its valleys running off it like spokes.
A cave that is a split rather than a dissolved passage, opened when the rock moved.
A bowl bitten out of a mountain head, usually with meltwater standing in the floor.
A knife edge between two hollows, wide enough to walk along and no wider.
A summit chewed to a point from three or more sides at once.
A ridge of dumped rubble marking how far the ice got before it gave up.
A long bank of debris along a valley side, dropped where the ice edge used to ride.
A dark stripe of rubble down the middle of the ice, where two flows joined.
A smooth whaleback hill, steep at one end and tapered away at the other.
A winding gravel ridge that follows no valley, because it was a river inside the ice.
A lumpy mound of sorted sand and gravel let down when the ice around it melted.
A round hollow, often with water in it, where a buried block of ice finally went.
A wide flat wash of sand and gravel spread beyond the ice front by meltwater.
A rock knob smoothed on the side the ice came from and torn ragged on the other.
A boulder of the wrong rock entirely, set down where nothing like it belongs.
A trough with a flat floor and steep sides, far too big for the stream now in it.
A side valley left stranded high above the main floor, its stream falling out of it.
A crag standing clear of the ice sheet, the only bare ground for miles around.
The high line where the ice sheet parts and flows two different ways.
A river of ice draining the sheet through a gap, crevassed all the way down.
A blue tunnel melted through the ice by running water, and still being melted.
A shaft in the ice that swallows a meltwater stream whole and drops it out of sight.
A drowned ice-cut trough: deep water with a wall on either side and no beach at all.
Ice floating on sea, thick enough to stand on and flat to the horizon.
A collapsed limestone shaft flooded to the water table.
A network of dissolved passages, some walkable and most not, going further than anyone has.
A funnel in the ground where the roof of something underneath came down.
A wide flat-floored basin ringed by limestone hills, farmed in summer and flooded in winter.
Bare rock split into blocks by deep grooves, with whole plants living down in the cracks.
A window where an underground river shows itself for a few paces, then goes back under.
The hole a surface stream disappears into, and does not come back out of.
A vertical shaft dropping straight into the dark, with no ledge to start from.
A steep-sided limestone stack rising sheer out of flat ground, wooded on top.
A raw channel cut into soft ground, deepening every storm and safe to cross nowhere.
A standing column of soft rock left behind because a harder cap protected it.
A ridge carved along the wind's line, streamlined like a hull left on the desert floor.
A crack you can touch both walls of, dark at noon and lethal when it rains upstream.
A gently sloping rock apron running out from the hills under a thin skin of gravel.
A lone dome of hard rock standing out of the plain, visible a day's walk away.
A shallow basin the wind has scooped out down to where the ground holds damp.
A scooped recess in a cliff face, dry underneath and out of the weather.
A span of rock left standing over a gap after the stream cut through beneath it.
Sand to the horizon in ranks, each crest moving a little every year.
A crescent of sand with its horns pointed downwind, walking a few paces a year.
A long sharp-crested ridge of sand lying with the wind rather than across it.
A high mound with arms running off several ways, because the wind cannot decide.
Rank after rank of sand ridges set square across the wind, like a frozen swell.
A sand ridge so large that the ordinary dunes ride along on its back.
A floor of close-packed stones polished flat, the fine stuff all blown out between.
A dry lake bed cracked to a tile pattern, sheet water for one week in a year.
A salt-crusted coastal flat where the water table sits just under a treacherous crust.
A dry stone channel that is a road most of the year and a torrent for one afternoon.
A continuous slope of merged gravel fans running the whole foot of a range.
Ground littered with stones the blown sand has cut into facets and hard edges.
Water reaching the surface where nothing else does, and everything alive for miles at it.
A white glaring plain that crunches underfoot and bleeds brine where it breaks.
Dunes of pale crystal sand, cool to the hand where ordinary sand would burn.
A rock face gone black-brown with age, old marks cut through it to lighter stone.
Hummocks of sand each anchored by one stubborn bush, scoured bare in between.
A rock ridge undercut by sand-blast, standing on a narrower foot than its top.
Flat wind-laid sand with no dunes at all: easy going, and the same in every direction.
A broad low mountain of runny flows, so gentle you are on it before you notice.
A steep layered peak of ash and lava, symmetrical enough to look built on purpose.
A small loose heap of cinder with a crater in the top, still warm in places.
The flat floor of a mountain that emptied itself and fell in.
A drained tunnel the flow left behind when its crust set and its middle ran on.
A field of black clinker that will take a pair of boots apart in an afternoon.
Rope-coiled black rock, smooth enough to walk on and glassy enough to cut.
A hole breathing sulphur steam, with yellow crystals grown round its lip.
A wall of welded blobs built along a fissure where the fountain once played.
The hard throat of a dead volcano, left standing after the cone around it went.
A low ash rampart round a wide shallow crater, usually with water in the middle.
A spread of grey mud and boulders that came down a valley at once and set hard.
A crack in the ground running straight for miles, with warm air coming out of it.
The line where the fall stopped: grey to one side, green to the other, and nothing between.
Soft grey ground that takes a bootprint and keeps it until the next fall covers it.
Grass and channel by turns, walkable at low water and not at high.
Low turf cut by creeks that fill with sea; grazed in summer, under water in a surge.
A tangle of stilt roots standing in salt mud, impassable except by the tide channels.
Standing reed higher than a person, water underfoot, and paths only where it is cut.
A dome of peat that has grown above the water table and drinks nothing but rain.
Peat laid over everything, hill and hollow alike, wet enough to swallow a boot.
A ragged bank of bare peat where the surface tore open and started washing away.
Trees standing in water, with the ground somewhere below and no telling where.
Wet scrub of willow and alder, thorny, and slower to cross than open water.
Ground that is meadow in one season and shallow lake in another, without warning.
A patch kept permanently wet by water rising from below, greener than all round it.
A raft of roots and moss lying on open water, taking weight until it does not.
A bare salt patch inside the marsh where nothing grows and the crust holds water.
Ground that shivers for several paces around every footfall, because it is floating.
New marsh grown on the river's freshest deposits, changing shape within a lifetime.
Reed and salt grass mixed together where a lagoon is neither sea nor river.
Grass that stays green all summer because the water is never far under it.
A small cold lake sitting in a rock bowl, fed by snow and nothing else.
Deep still water filling an old vent, steep walls all round and one way down.
A long narrow lake in a glacial trough, deeper than it has any right to be.
Water held back by a bank of loose rubble that was never built to hold anything.
A new lake behind a hillside that came down across the valley and stayed there.
A lake with no outlet, so everything the rivers bring stays and concentrates.
Water too salty to drink and heavy enough to float in, rimmed all round with white.
A lake whose depths never mix with its surface; nothing lives down there at all.
A place on the lake bed that steams, with dead fish and warm water above it.
A flat shelf built out into the lake where a river drops what it was carrying.
An old waterline cut round the basin, level for miles, from when the lake stood higher.
Water wide enough to have weather of its own, with no way out to the ocean.
A shallow sheet that appears after rain, breeds a season's life, and dries.
A ring of low reef islands round a lagoon, with nothing but ocean outside it.
A steep green island built on its own cone, with cloud caught on the top of it.
An island of proper old rock: a piece of the mainland the sea got in between.
A bare rock the sea covers and uncovers; a hazard, never a landing.
A low sand islet sitting on the reef rim, a few palms and no fresh water on it.
A heap of coral sand built up on the reef flat, moved by every serious storm.
A wooded island standing inside its own reef, with quiet water all round it.
The flattest ground in the world, under more water than the light can cross.
A submerged mountain chain where new sea floor is made and pushed aside.
A drowned peak rising off the deep floor and stopping short of the surface.
A drowned peak with its top planed flat, from when it still stood up in the surf.
A long gash in the sea floor: the deepest water anywhere, and the coldest.
Living rock built right against the shore, breaking every swell before it lands.
A wall of living rock standing offshore with a channel of quiet water behind it.
A broad shallow platform of coral where the water goes suddenly pale.
A gorge cut into the shelf edge, funnelling everything that falls into the deep.
